maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT, 1934 CONTROL OF SHIPMENT OF MUNITIONS BY SHIPS REGISTERED IN CANADA

speechtext:
Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 9, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, 1934.
He said: This amendment to the Canada Shipping Act sets up machinery by means of which the government can control shipments in Canadian vessels of arms and war materials to belligerent countries if and when such control is deemed necessary.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, January 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. N. Francceur for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Bennett.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We are met, I believe, Mr. Speaker, in one of the gravest years in the history of our dominion. I think the events of the next year will abundantly prove that to be the case. Therefore I believe it is most important that all of us should work together with the greatest possible earnestness, forgetting such matters as political struggles. In the debate yesterday, although the speeches were excellent and amusing and fine displays of parliamentary oratory, there was altogether too much jockeying for political advantage. We
should cease endeavouring to gain political advantage at least while we are in this very trying time.
As a case in point of this political jockeying let me mention one instance. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) chose to interpret the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) as showing that he was opposed to foreign trade, and he concluded, I judge from his remarks, that the leader of the opposition was in agreement with the social credit group in attaching small value to foreign trade. Now I assume that the Prime Minister was sincere in that remark. If he was he manifested a lack of knowledge concerning social credit, for the social credit advocates have never disparaged the value of foreign trade. All they have done is to urge upon the people that we must not look to foreign trade alone for the complete solution of our problems. Perhaps it would be instructive if I were to read one or two little quotations. I do not wish to read quotations to any extent this year, but since this matter has been raised it is of vital importance that the country should know just where the social credit people stand. First I should like to refer to Major Douglas himself, as the founder of the movement. I am quoting from his book called Economic Democracy, at page 145, where I read these words:
It must be evident therefore that an economic system involving forced extrusion of product from the community producing, as an integral component of the machinery for the distribution of purchasing power, is entirely incompatible with any effective league of nations, because the logical and inevitable end of economic competition is war.
That was what I understood the right hon. leader of the opposition to contend, and that is our contention. Trade, of course; if we have a surplus of wheat and another country has a surplus of bananas, of course trade the surplus of wheat for the surplus of bananas. But if the people producing apples wish to trade their apples for our beef; if we already have apples and we not only refuse to accept their product but go into the world market and endeavour to displace their product with our apples, then we put them in a position which ultimately will lead to war. There can be no question regarding that.
In order that everyone may see that this belief is held by the Canadian social credit movement let me quote a statement of the Douglas Social Credit Bureau of Canada, with headquarters in Ottawa. I am not saying that this organization is identical with the one which I represent, although I see no difference between the two. I am merely quoting what is

The Address-Mr. Blachmore
said here. This statement is issued under date of February 1, 1938. and bears exactly upon the situation under consideration:
Under a social credit administration foreign trade would he distinctly encouraged hut the transactions between countries would he balanced. There would he no need for the so-called "favourable balance of trade.1' Imports to Canada would be a distinct advantage, for under social credit adequate purchasing power would be distributed to enable Canadians to purchase the imports, thereby increasing the standard of living and diversifying the products available.
Imported goods are, so far as real wealth is concerned, equivalent to goods produced by home industry and exported goods are equivalent to goods consumed. [DOT]	.
Under existing conditions one nation can only expand its foreign market at the expense of other nations; and as an expanding market is, under the present system, a matter of life and death for all nations, the ensuing scramble for markets inevitably culminates in war.
Ralph L. Duclos, President.
I 'believe, Mr. Speaker, that these extracts sufficiently clarify the position of those who believe in social credit with respect to trade, and I maintain that any attempt to misrepresent to the people of this country the meaning of the contentions of the followers of social credit is an action distinctly contrary to the interests of Canada. If we want the truth-[DOT] and as the Prime Minister very well said, we do want the truth-certainly that is not the way to get it. I support both those statements, without making any statement myself with regard to trade, except that I endorse the remarks and the sentiments contained in those two excerpts.
Perhaps I may be just a little more truculent than usual because for two years in the province of Alberta we have experienced the most deliberate, the most malicious, the most unjustifiable attempt to drag all sorts and kinds of red herrings across the path. Anything and everything that could foe done to deceive the people has been done. No attempt at all has been made to give them the truth. We may laugh about that, but that is the fact, and it can be verified over and over again. I am not going to bring up any unpleasant matters this afternoon, but that statement stands. If we want the truth there is a way to get it. I cannot recall the exact words used last night by the Prime Minister but, as he said, the truth will stand and it is the truth we want.

speechtext: How about the twenty-five dollars?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is another bit of it. Isn't that a brilliant attempt to get the truth?
I was impressed with the remark of the leader of the opposition with regard to righteous elections. I believe that statement,

although it was not pleasant, raised a question which the people of this dominion must settle, or, as the right hon. gentleman said, our very national existence is endangered. What do we mean by democracy? Do we not mean an appeal to the people so that the people, informed, intelligent and calm, may through their ballots express a considered opinion as to the policy which the government should follow in carrying on the affairs of the country? Is that not what we wish? All we need do is just think of what has been done in far, far too many constituencies throughout this country, in order to realize that the policy pursued by both the old line parties has been diametrically opposed to that, the object being under all conditions to deceive the people and confuse them so they do not know what it is all about.
I come from a province, Mr. Speaker, where we have grappled with this problem with great earnestness since 1921. In that year we commenced to fight our elections with the nickels and dimes of the people. The social credit victory in 1935 was won almost with the very lifeblood of the people, and since those sacrifices were made by poor, suffering men and women, in order to get a government which would represent them, we have had attempts made to override the will of the people by the most despicable forms of deception. We know what democracy is. We started this thing in 1921 and we have continued it even to the present time. Every cent that is used to fight a social credit election in Alberta comes out of the pockets of the poorest people in the province, fighting earnestly for the right to live and believing still in the principles of democracy.
The propaganda which has gone on and is going on to-day in the province of Alberta is a standing disgrace to the people of this dominion. I say that without fear of any kind of successful contradiction. We are seeing perpetrated upon the people of that province and the people of the whole dominion a monstrous iniquity. Somewhere there is a solution to our problems. Do you know where the solution is? If the answer were to be given from your own soul it would be, "No, I do not; I wish to heaven I did." How are we going to find that solution if we persist in discrediting everyone who comes forward with a new idea? Political trickery has been resorted to. I had not intended to mention the subject. However, the right hon. the leader of the opposition raised the question, and I believe I should make some observations. Out in our province there exists a government duly elected by the considered thought of the people of Alberta. Every

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
conceivable device has been exercised to prevent that government from doing what the people put it there to do. This summer there was formed a despicable organization called the People's League, very aptly called by Premier Aberhart the people's slavery league. That is exactly what it is. In that league were participating the Liberal and Conservative leaders of the province. In it were found some leaders in the United Farmers of Alberta group, and some others. There is no gainsaying that fact; there it is.
At least partially as a result of the operations of this organization Mr. E. L. Gray was elected in Edmonton as a representative of the People's League. Then they turned to the provincial constituency of Lethbridge, and by a sufficiency of red herring dragging, and the exercise of other devices beneath my notice, they succeeded in electing another People's League candidate. Three days following his election Mr. E. L. Gray, on behalf of himself and the Liberal party, withdrew from the combination. He was completely disgusted with its behaviour. However they had succeeded in electing two men, and the elections were noised across the country as evidence that the Aberhart administration was losing the confidence of the people of Alberta.
I ask any fair minded man or woman in the house, and I realize that all hon. members could be so classed, if he or she regards that as decent procedure in Canada. Is it in accordance with what you consider sound behaviour on the part of men who pose as the leaders? That is all I ask; you need not answer it, but just think it over.
May I now proceed to. mention some misrepresentation which took place last night. I shall not say it was deliberate; I am almost certain it was unconscious. However there was at least the intimation, or something which gave me the impression, whether the Prime Minister meant it that way or not, that he attributed the unrest in Canada, in which five of our majestic provinces have participated, to ill will which exists in other parts of the world. He has suggested that that ill will has come into our country and that we have become contaminated with it. Well, that may be a good political move, but in my judgment it is as far from the truth as it could possibly be. I shall not say it was a deliberate misrepresentation, but I must say that it manifested a great lack of consideration.
Before dealing with this matter at greater length may I refer for a few moments to the
kind words used by the leader of the opposition in advocating some of the avowed principles which we hold dear.

speechtext:
No doubt there may be a good deal of merriment in that connection. There was a time, however, when the principle of the abolition of slavery in the English speaking world was laughed at. They laughed at that time, just as hon. members across the chamber have laughed today. Because there were men and women who stood out sternly and self-sacrificingly through the years in the defence of those principles, they finally prevailed. The same is true with respect to the secret ballot, and in connection with many principles which today we value and prize, and which make our democratic institutions both beautiful and hopeful. So it is with the principles I put before the house. The day will come when all will recognize that, absurd as they may seem today, those principles are sound.
I know not why the right hon. the leader of the opposition made the statements to which I have referred, but no matter why he made them I wish to thank him for them. If he has come to see the light, it is greatly to his credit. I wish to give credit where credit is due.
Before commencing a discussion of the causes of the strains and stresses which are so painfully manifested in the dominion I should like briefly to deal with the question of recovery. Speaking generally I find it beyond my power to comprehend why men as intelligent, thoughtful and well informed as hon. members sitting opposite can be satisfied with such specious reasoning regarding recovery. I was positively amazed to hear some of the observations made yesterday, and especially when one can find from any informed source a complete confutation of every statement that was made.
For example, there is not one of the South American republics which has not had as satisfactory recovery as has Canada, and during the very years in which the Liberal administration has held office in this country. The little country of Chile, which was looked upon as the most hopeless spot in a hopeless world, after the crisis of 1931, has had a phenomenal recovery. Was that because the Liberal party were in power in Canada? Let us be at least careful. Let us spend our time at something profitable. Let us face realities.
According to the best authorities the reason for recovery was the very rapid increase in rearmament. Around fifteen billions of dollars
The Address-Mr. Blackmore

is being poured out to-day by the various nations of the world, and the demands for raw materials which can be turned into war machinery are tremendous. Those demands have melted or, shall we say, unfrozen the great masses of goods which were waiting for buyers. As a result of that change the countries have felt free to lower their tariff restrictions and to begin to trade. There can be no successful contradiction of that statement. I could quote authorities which could not be disregarded by any person who has any interest in his reputation for accuracy. I could quote authorities in our own country. We could turn to the report of the 106th annual meeting of the Bank of Nova Scotia held recently, which was published in the Ottawa Citizen of January 28. There it is stated clearly that the recovery was due to rearmament, and that it is general throughout the world.
How in the world can men arrogate to themselves or to their party complete credit for the achievement of something which is world wide. In the same report there is the statement that to a great degree economic conditions in Canada are dependent upon those in the United States. Witness recently the depression in Canada, and the recession which began in the United States on August 15. To say that one political party in Canada has solved an economic problem, and caused recovery, is reckless and beyond excusability.
Then, there is a further difficulty which has to be considered, I value optimism. We could not live without it; but let us be careful of our optimism. Around us to-day there are signs of recession. According to the figures which I have, already in the United States thirty billion dollars worth of wealth has been swept away. In Great Britain we find that between November 15 and December 15. 1937, unemployment was increased by 166,204. Notwithstanding that their armament preparation race is at its' height and their re-housing program is under way, there were 90,000 more unemployed in December 1937 than there were in December 1936. There is a reason for this increase in the number of unemployed; let us try to find it. Some may say that the occurrence was seasonal, but such is not the fact. In 1936, from November 15 to December 15, there was an increase of 30,000 in the number employed, but for the same period in this year we find a decrease of 166.204. Any one who desires to be at all judicious must bear these facts in mind before he rushes to make any reckless confMr. Blackmore.]
elusion. Evidence of this statement may be found in the Christian Science Monitor of January 22, at page 9.
What was the cause of the recession in the United States? I am not going to take the time to discuss the matter at any length, but I should like to direct the attention of such hon. members as may not have noticed it to the October, 1937, letter of the Royal Bank of Canada. There they will find a well-developed analysis of the situation by a careful thinker. He shows that whereas in 1936 the President of the United States put that country into debt to the extent of 14,500,000,000, scattering the money around generously through the WPA and CCC programs, yet increasing the purchasing power of the people, in 1937 he changed his policy considerably. In that year he went into debt to the extent of only $1,500,000,000, and the result was the beginning of a depression the end of which no one can see. Does that not show that the secret of recovery or of avoiding depression is the spending of money? About half way down in the second column of his letter this gentleman sets forth this principle. I shall just quote a few words out of their context, but the meaning is as I have given it. He states:
It would seem that the government will be compelled to increase its spending or, as an alternative, to permit a decline in national income.
Where will the government get the money to spend? If it must borrow that money, then it will be creating a disaster because the debt is already beyond the power of the people to pay under the present economic system. How can the United States ward off a fall in the national income in the midst of the greatest era of prosperity this world has ever seen? That is the problem we are facing, but I am going to leave it at that.
There is another matter which I think should be considered carefully. Last year I supported the government in its move to rearm for Canada's defence. I am confident that that was a wise move and I think the evidence is that we were sound in our judgment. I did not take the occasion to point out at that time to the house that I am unalterably opposed to war. I did not point out that I believed that some time we are going to have the fulfilment of that great scriptural passage wherein the prophet says:
-and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
If the time has not come when we can do that, when do hon. members of this house think it will come? How can we do it, is

When I consider .that every dollar's worth of that material is helping the Japanese to destroy the Chinese I fail to be warmed with any enthusiasm when contemplating that increase in our trade.
Here is another thing which I believe hon. members will find interesting. I intend to spend most of my time in discussing this matter .because, after all, it is dear to my heart. I am not a pacifist in the sense that I want peace at any price. I realize that we must have some defence, but I realize also that there are fundamental causes of war which people of our intelligence should be able to discover. An effort should be made to remove these causes but we probably do not realize what they are.
Let us consider why Japan is attacking China. The information I have is up to date as far as I have been able to find out. The area of Japan is 150,000 square miles and her population totals 70,000,000 people. She has 2,900 people per square mile of area. Hon. members of this house need only think of what it would mean to have 2,900 people for every square mile of their constituencies. Then take Great Britain, with a population of 2.200 to every square mile; or China, with 1,300 people to every square mile.

I have mentioned
only three. The figures I have quoted give
us a picture of the conditions Japan is struggling against, and I am going to ask hon. members now, frankly: Can you see how in the world international trade is going to help Japan-the kind of international trade that we are getting? Just let us see.
The resources of Japan comprise the following, and all this has a bearing on the question: Japan has small coal deposits; considerable iron ore, of a poor quality; some copper, and some water power, about one-fifth of the amount Canada has. She cannot send her people abroad, so that emigration is no solution for her difficulties. What is her solution? Manifestly, she must import raw materials, manufacture them and sell the finished products in the markets of the world. We know-we have the figures brought to our attention-at what ridiculous prices Japan has been able to sell her products abroad. For example, she can sell at as low as $6, a bicycle that we would sell here for $50, and she is doing that in an attempt to get into world markets. We have raised tariff barriers against her. "Very well," the free traders will say, "that is where our trade will come in." Yes, but wait a moment. When these Japanese bicycles come to our shores, it is found that we are already manufacturing bicycles, and instead of lowering our tariffs to admit bicycles we raise our tariffs to keep them out. The result is that Japanese have turned from us in desperation, and that has gone to the point where it has maddened the people of Japan.
Here are figures which I have found astonishing, of Japanese imports and exports, showing that her balance of trade has been getting rapidly worse since 1931. Taking 100 as a basis for 1931-these figures will show her difficulty in maintaining a balance of trade in her favour-the index figure stood at 89 in 1932, 83 in 1933, 73 in 1934, 71 in 1935, and 68 in 1936. It was time Japan did something, was it not?
I am going to ask frankly, what were we doing to help Japan? In the light of what I have quoted from Major Douglas, and the Ottawa Social Credit Bureau, I ask what were we doing to help Japan? If we were not consciously courting war, we were certainly doing it unconsciously. The figures I have quoted mean that in 1936 Japan had to give for the same quantity of imports, 47 per cent more, in quantity of exports, than she gave in 1931. Now we see why the right hon. leader of the opposition says that our cutthroat competition will cause war.
My time is rapidly expiring, but before I sit down there is one extremely important

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
point upon which I wish to touch, and that is the causes of the strains and stresses. I shall not have time to develop this subject at any length today, but in future discussions I a,m going to rise and lay before you, my fellow-Canadians, as an advocate from the province of Alberta coming here to plead in the interests of justice before the high court of parliament, the reasons why we are forced to make these strains and stresses that we are making-and they have nothing to do with ill will against any other country, I can tell you that.
In the first place, this government has not removed poverty. I aiji not saying that under the existing financial structure they could do any better than they are doing. In fact, I am pleased with the progress this government has made under the existing financial structure. But I say that your financial structure is wrong, fundamentally wrong, and you will never solve your problems until you change that financial structure, whether you think so or not.
The possibilities which we have at the present time make it a disgrace to us to consider the continued existence of poverty in our midst. Take the Brookings Institution discoveries. It has found that in the peak of the boom in the United States, the people of that country were able to buy only eighty per cent of the productive capacity of the United States. Now, will any member of this house, who thinks he knows, tell us why that was? Without any addition to their industrial equipment or any addition to their labour, they would have been able to increase their production thirty per cent. Will anybody who thinks he knows tell us why they did not do it? You only need to become aware of these things and the very blood in your veins begins to boil.
A similar condition existed in Canada. There is no question about the facts which I have given from this report. Our wage level is a disgrace considering our opportunities. In 1935, according to Mr. Horace L. Seymour, B.A., B.Sc., writing in the Canadian Unionist for November, 1937, sixty per cent of the Ontario workers receive less than $900 a year. Keep that figure of 1900 in mind until we get some more facts and see how it makes you feel about the way your province and your dominion is being managed. The United States government, on July 11, 1937, issued to the press a report in which it was set forth that a family of four in the United States required $30 per week, if they were 
to live decently. Now living conditions in the United States are easier than they are here.

government made the statement that in order to live decently at all a family required $1,250 a year. All you need to do is to think of the contemptible pittance you are giving your unemployed; think of the disgracefully low income which your people are receiving for their work; think of the starvation income upon which your farming population has to live; and then you will see what I contend without any fear of successful contradiction, that your standard of living is far lower than it needs to be.
I am going to say only one thing more in closing. I am leaving out a great deal that I had intended to say, which I shall have to leave for another occasion. Here is a man you may not agree with. Here is Professor R. F. Irvine, M.A., for twenty-five years professor of economics at Sydney university, Australia, an orthodox professor of economics, and he solemnly uses these words in 1933:
I believe that the principles put forward by C. H. Douglas are not only sound, but that they provide the only practical way of escape from the tragic fate which otherwise awaits the whole of western civilization.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I heartily concur in the protest of the last speaker (Mr. Blackmore) against the shipment of materials of war from Canada to Japan, and we shall take an early opportunity of bringing this matter before the house.
I shall not attempt to follow the arguments advanced in the Prime Minister's lengthy speech; I am afraid it would take more than my forty minutes to correct some of the implications of his statements. He assumes that revenue is an index of prosperity; I suggest it may be only an indication of oppressive taxation. He assumes that the total production or national income means the general welfare; it may mean simply the opportunity for the wealthier to become still more wealthy. He assumes that the total volume of trade is an indication of national greatness; it may simply show how thoroughly we are being exploited.

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
I agree heartily with the wording of the amendment as proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I should like to congratulate the Conservatives on their seeming conversion; possibly our efforts throughout the years have not been altogether wasted.
The speech itself seems to run true to form- Liberal form. There is very little constructive legislation adumbrated. We are told that there is to be sought an amendment to the British North America Act to enable the dominion government to enact a national scheme of unemployment insurance. But why should we not ask for an amendment that would give us the right to amend our own constitution in any way we may please; or better still, why not assert that we have such a right? Where are all the fine phrases of the imperial conference of 1926? You will recall this language in reference to the self-governing communities:
They are autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown and freely associated as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
After all that, we are going, cap in hand, asking that we may be allowed the right to amend our constitution in one particular. I hope that some day in Canada we shall acquire a little bit of dignity. I wish the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) could have given a lead in that direction.
I was almost hoping that we might have had in the speech some reference to safeguarding the civil rights of our people. Very shortly before the close of the last session I *brought to the attention of the government the serious curtailment of our civil liberties through the so-called "padlock law" of Quebec. I may say that our worst apprehensions have been realized; for between November 9, 1937, when the law was enacted, and January 27, 1938, the act has been applied some fifty times. Let me show what that means in the individual home.
A few days ago I had a personal letter from a friend of mine whom I had known many years ago in the west when she was engaged in social service activities. She wrote telling me that her home had been raided by the provincial police. I quote a paragraph:
They didn't get any of the works of Marx or Lenin but they took your biography and a number of social research pamphlets. They also took a book on Spinoza written by a young Columbia professor whom I know, with his autograph in it, so I'm afraid Mr. Duplessis and his friends are not up on the fine points of the Labour movement. Among other subversive literature they took a copy of the magazine "Time" which happened to have Leon
Trotsky's picture on the back of it and another dangerous bit they got was a copy of "Current History." I was able to rescue a book on the South Seas by Robert Louis Stevenson and also a novel by Dostoyefsky.
They found a book of German Fairy Tales and were quite surprised that we could read Yiddish.
Apparently the provincial police had confused German and Yiddish. This is simply typical of the class of literature that has been seized in recent months in the homes of Canadian people in the province of Quebec.
I have here a list which I will not take time to read. I ask, have we no right to expect that the government of Canada will protect its citizens? I called attention on March 30 to this situation. Let me read a summary of my position. I said:
I would ask in closing: What might we expect from the Minister of Justice in a Liberal cabinet? First of all, I think a declaration that the Quebec act is ultra vires and as illegal as a sit-down strike. In the one instance the minister undertook to interpret the law; why should he not do so in this much more important case?
Second, we might expect a statement that there are legitimate means of protecting Quebec against lawlessness and violence. We have that, as I think he will tell us, in the criminal code. . . .
Third, there should be the emphatic assurance that the resources of the dominion will be used to protect the rights and liberties of all Canadian citizens-even in Quebec. . . .
Fourth, I suggest that the minister should assure us that there will be a reference to the supreme court in order that we may know what rights we have. I point out once more that such action was taken by the government in, respect to certain social security measures. Surely similar action might be taken in the present instance.
What had the minister to say in reply? He pleaded that the bill had not come formally before him. Surely he cannot any longer make that plea. Secondly, as regards disallowance as a possible course of action, he said:
For many years the power of disallowance lias not been resorted to by the government of Canada. . . .
I would not say the same condition would apply to provincial legislation, but it has often been stated by the courts that within the sphere of their own jurisdiction the provincial legislatures are sovereign. I do not think that in a federation such as this the power of disallowance could easily be exercised by the central government. I believe the provincial legislatures feel that they are still supreme and sovereign within the sphere of their jurisdiction.
Since that -time the power of disallowance has been exercised by the dominion in the case of Alberta. If it can be done with respect to Alberta when it concerns financial

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
measures, why not with respect to Quebec when the matter concerns the liberties of the citizen? The minister goes on to say:
The hon. member suggests that there should be a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. As I have said, I was surprised to hear him make that statement, because he criticized the government for having referred to the Supreme Court of Canada acts of our own parliament; now he wants us to take an act of the legislature of Quebec and refer it to the supreme court. All I can say with regard to his suggestion-and the hon. member certainly does not expect me to say more-is that it will receive the most serious consideration.
Well, there have been some eight or nine months for consideration, so I should like the Minister of Justice to take an early opportunity of informing the house what action the government propose to take to safeguard the interests of our citizens in the province of Quebec.
With regard to the economic situation, the speech from the throne says;
It is gratifying to note that, during the past year, there has been a further substantial advance in Canada's economic recovery.
I suggest that that sounds very much like the echo of a bank president's annual address. The yardstick used is the same, that is, increased resources and expanding trade. I should like to suggest that prosperity in Canada is very spotty indeed. There are many of our communities that have not experienced the slightest return of prosperity. It is unfortunately my duty to present the darker side of the picture. The position of my own constituents, which is that of vast numbers of people throughout the country, shows that there is anything but prosperity at the present moment. Take the case of my own city of Winnipeg. We in the west have recently had to prepare some statistics in regard to this matter, so fortunately the facts are available. I quote from the submission of the city of Winnipeg to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations:
Up to the end of 1936, property abandoned by the former owners and reverted to the city through tax sale procedure was valued at $7,500,000, and represents over 33 per cent of the area of the city. In addition properties valued at $6,400,000 have been sold for tax arrears, but have not yet come into the city's hands.
Or again;
Many properties in good condition have been demolished by the owners in order to escape taxation. These include residences of the class which may he termed the mansion type, amongst which were the former homes of such well known citizens as Sir Augustus Nanton, Sir William Whyte, Sir Daniel McMillan, the Honourable Robert Rogers, and so on. A number of other houses of the same type have been

abandoned by the owners and are now owned by the city. In addition many business properties have been torn down including the former Hudson's Bay departmental store on Main street, occupying half a city block. It is also significant that title through tax sale proceedings has or can be taken to many valuable business properties situated in the very heart of the city, including Robinson's department store, almost at the corner of Main street and Portage avenue, the Forum block, the Walker theatre, the Playhouse theatre, and many warehouse and other properties. Each of these properties have been at one time valued at over $100,000 at least, and some of them at very much more.
Or again:
Salaries and wages of all employees, including teachers, have been reduced on the average by about 15 per cent.
Or again:
Many essential services, including street maintenance, the provision of adequate fire protection equipment, etc., have had to be neglected. The amount expended in 1936 for those services fell short of normal requirements bv at least $300,000.
Or again:
The Bank of Canada report finds that there is not now available, for either the city or the province, new sources of revenue through taxation.
And again:
The Bank of Canada in its report on the finances of the province made early this year states that Winnipeg on account of being the chief urban centre of the west has been called on to bear a disproportionate share of the relief burden. The report goes on to say that eighty-four per cent of all direct relief expenditures in the province have had to be made in Winnipeg and suburbs. An analysis of Winnipeg relief cases made some months ago showed that of 6.837 families on relief 959, or fourteen per cent, had come to reside in Winnipeg since 1930.
And again:
The city has thus not only exhausted all sources of revenue, but has also reached the limit of its capacity to borrow for relief purposes, and unless aid is immediately forthcoming from the dominion or provincial governments, a major crisis will be inevitable at the end of the year.
These are serious statements, coming from the city of Winnipeg itself. As hon. members know, western cities do not like to advertise their poverty. Alderman E. D. Honey-man a few weeks ago-someone prompts me that he is a Liberal, but I was speaking of him in his capacity as alderman-speaking in committee of the whole of the legislature of Manitoba, stated that there were 5,000 families on relief, that eighty-five per cent of the cases were willing to work. I was not so greatly moved yesterday when I heard the

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
Prime Minister speaking of all the schemes the government has set up to help the unemployed. Of course these schemes are doing something, and I welcome them as far as they go, but they do not begin to touch the fringe of the unemployment problem in this country. I repeat that in my own city there are 5,000 families on relief, -and I may say that 1,000 of these are recent arrivals in the city, many of them from farming districts. And eighty-five per cent of the cases were willing to work. I should like the Minister of Labour to take an early opportunity of explaining a situation of -that kind, and bringing forward some adequate provision to meet the immediate needs of the unemployed. It is not sufficient to eay that there are fewer unemployed now than there were a year ago; that does not help -those who are to-day in the bread lines.
Again let me give a few facts with regard to the rural part of my own province. 1 fancy that people in the east hav-e not yet realized the condition of the rural west. I quote again from statistics given in Manitoba's -case as presented to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations. For the year ended June 30, 1937, it was estimated that there were 868 school teachers in Manitoba in receipt of a salary under $500 per year. These represent twenty per cent of the -total teaching force of the province and forty-two per cent of the rural teaching staff. School inspectors report rapid deterioration in school buildings owing to inability to finance repairs. They also report deficient equipment in a large number of schools. At the present time, mainly for financial reasons, 237 school districts are being administered by official trustees, and these districts have been operated on the average only 100 days yearly. In dealing with the municipal financial situation it was submitted that land, the main source of municipal taxation, could not bear any further burden of taxation.
The effect of this condition on individuals is indicated in another section of the same report. Surely matters of this kind are of as much importance as the fact that we are assuming a high position among the nations in the total volume of our trade. What are the social effects of the present situation throughout the province of Manitoba with respect to individuals?
(1)	Incomes have declined to a point below the average for Canada; and net profits from private enterprise in agriculture, except in the last two years, have in many cases disappeared;
(2)	For large numbers of our citizens, private indebtedness has been found too heavy to be
borne, necessitating the continuance of debt adjustment laws by the provincial government and of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act by the dominion;
(3)	For many taxpayers arrears of taxes are beyond their capacity to pay;
(4)	Production of agricultural products by farmers has been maintained largely by drawing upon capital reserves, by permitting -heavy depreciation in equipment, by dispensing with all but a minimum of hired labour, by a large degree of dependence upon family labour, and by a distinct lowering of living standards;
(5)	To many individuals opportunity for employment lias disappeared; a long repetition of disappointments has brought discouragement, loss of hope of improvement in economic conditions and the acceptance by some of radical views which find expression in various forms of political protest, in the hope that a change might bring about better conditions.
Again let me remind hon. members that these are by no means irresponsible statements. I think they may be taken to represent the facts of the situation.
At this time I shall not go into the proposals that the government of -my province make with regard to the provincial debt and interest burden or with regard to the allocation of responsibilities as between the dominion and the provincial governments. I pass on for a moment to the question of unemployment, and in view of the facts that I have related with regard to my own city and province, -which might be supplemented by the facts with regard to unemployment in other provinces, I ask what effective action is being taken by this government that has been in office now for two or three yeans. The other day I came across a pamphlet entitled The Vo-ice of the People, a reprint of the statements issued to the press by Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King on the night of the general election, October 14, 1935, and issued by the National Liberal Federation of Canada, 114 Wellington street, Ottawa. I quote:
To-day's election discloses that the people share the view which the Liberal party has all along maintained, that unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem.
It was the pledge to deal with unemployment, according to the Prime Minister's own statement, that elected the Liberals to office. A few weeks ago we had the interim report of the national employment commission, which recommended that the primary responsibility for the relief of distress should remain with the municipal authority and/or the province. So here, after two years, it is a case of "as you were." Back again goes the responsibility upon the provinces and municipalities which, as far as the west is concerned, are absolutely unable to carry those burdens. Forgotten seems -to be the "work

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
and wages" program. Even relief is now considered as primarily a municipal or provincial program. Of course it may be said that this is simply the report of a commission and that it need not necessarily be the policy of the government. I hope that may prove to be true, but I very much fear that a report by a commission along this line will be considered to have absolved the government from directly undertaking the burden of unemployment and relief.
The problem is still acute. I shall not take time to read the figures, but I would point out that according to the interim report of the national commission, relief for unemployment can come only through measures that involve dominion government action. I give several points mentioned in the report:
In fact, the stage was in considerable measure already set for recovery since stocks of consumers' goods and raw materials had fallen to normal, or were well on the way to becoming normal;	_
Community savings had again accumulated and capital was beginning to press for investment;	.
Banking policy had resulted in low interest rates;
Abandonment of the gold standard had put the Canadian dollar on a more or less comparable basis with that of its competitors in the production of goods for export;
An increase in the price of gold and the discovery of new gold mining areas was proving a stimulus almost equivalent to that provided by an entirely new industry;
An accumulation of obsolescence in plant and equipment was becoming increasingly evident.
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that these are factors that do not come under the control of the provincial governments. They come under the control of the federal government. I am not now saying that the Liberal government is wholly to blame for this situation; not at all. I think the former government was very much to blame, especially in the case of the gold standard, but I do say that the recognition that these are factors that enter into the unemployment situation is clear evidence that the dominion government cannot escape responsibility with regard to the question of unemployment.
There is a very interesting passage that occurs in another section of Manitoba's case, in which reference is made to the effect of federal monetary policy on western Canadian economy:
To the seller of goods abroad, however, there are two factors that determine the price the seller receives for his production. These two factors are: first, the price of goods in the foreign import country, and, second, the rate of exchange. The rate of exchange is equally important in determining how much that price yields him in his own country.

In a preceding section I find this passage;
-the annual income to the grain growers of Manitoba upon their grain exports was $6,000,000 less than if the Canadian dollar had been kept in line with the Australian pound.
I submit that keeping the Canadian dollar in line with the Australian pound is not a matter than can be affected by any action the province might take. It is a dominion affair, and the effect of a wrong policy on the part of the dominion government has tended to worsen conditions in the west. Hence I think the dominion government is clearly responsible.
Let me make one other reference from Manitoba's case, and that is the effect of the federal tariff policy on western Canadian economy. It is very strange, Mr. Speaker, that it should fall to me to present this phase of the matter to a Liberal government. I should like to know why the Liberal members from the west are not doing it. I hope they will take an early opportunity to present this phase of the case, because remember, this Manitoba case is in effect presented by a Liberal government-a progressive Liberal government, if you like to call it that. I would hope that the case for the west with regard to lower tariffs would be backed up by the western Liberal members.
There are one or two passages in the statement that I should like to present. The right hon. leader of the opposition quoted the Minister of Labour. I shall not further embarrass him by quoting anything he said with regard to Nova Scotia. However, I shall quote the following from Manitoba's case:
The following tabulation brings together the results of our detailed calculations by commodity groups of the estimated increased cost per farm in western Canada due to tariff on
imports from the United States:
Automotive equipment and fuel.	.. $ 27	19Machinery, implements, etc	
18	45Building material	
7	16Household equipment and furniture	12	00Clothing	
24	41Food	
20	57Total	$110 38
There are approximately 290,000 farms in the three prairie provinces and we have estimated the added cost per farm per year as roughly $100. Therefore, the total added cost borne by western farmers is 29 million dollars per year.
The weight of this burden may be judged by the following comparisons: The total municipal and school tax burden in western Canada was 44-5 million dollars in 1933. This figure includes city, town, and village taxes. It is no exaggeration to state, therefore, that the cost of the tariff, to farmers only, is equal to what the whole population of western Canada now pays to maintain local government and education. The Searle Index calculates the average real property tax on western farms at $69.85, which, if compared with our estimates of an

The Address-Mr. Deachman
added tariff cost per farm of $100, indicates the relative weight on rural life of local taxes as compared with the burden of national tariff policy.
I would urge that it is high time that we no longer allow matters of monetary and tariff policy to drift, when they affect so adversely large sections of our community.
As I look over the speech from the throne I can find no indication of anything along new lines which would materially affect the welfare of the great masses of our people. To me that is the most serious aspect of the situation. Apparently we have gotten into a rut. Comfortably situated in Ottawa, we seem to be content to go over and over great masses of figures. We do not realize what they mean in terms of human welfare and human suffering.
A short time ago I came across a report in the New York Tribune of an address on the constitution delivered by President Roosevelt. It is not without application to conditions in Canada. It states:
The constitution of the United States was a layman's document, not a lawyer's contract.
I suggest that if the British North America Act is to be considered a lawyer's contract, in spite of the suffering which must be endured by a great number of our people, partly at least because of the inflexibility of that document, then there is a bad lookout for Canada. Mr. Roosevelt continued:
Less than two years ago fifty-eight of the highest priced lawyers in the land gave the nation, without cost to the nation, a solemn and formal opinion that the Wagner Labor Relations Act was unconstitutional, and in a few months the supreme court overruled them.
I would invite the attention of the Minister of Justice to that statement. Are we to go on indefinitely allowing our people to suffer economically because there was a constitution drawn up some seventy years ago which may have been fitted to the needs of our forefathers, but is not fitted to the needs of Canada to-day? One concluding pregnant sentence is this:
We will no longer be permitted to sacrifice each generation in turn while the law catches up with life. We can no longer afford the luxury of twenty-year lags.
I commend that to the attention of the Minister of Justice. I commend it to the attention of my legal friends in the house, and indeed to all others. We in Canada have been affording ourselves the luxury, here referred to as "twenty-year lags." We have been going along with old economic policies as well as an old constitution. Meantime the world has been moving with wonderful rapidity. Our people have suffered because the house and parliament has not had imagination enough to alter its policies to meet the new needs which this century has thrust upon us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always listen with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). He is a man of great faith. This is an age of grave doubts, and we must at least have some admiration for those men who still retain some of their old faith.
Almost three years ago the Social Credit party in Alberta was elected, with great promises. I venture to suggest that no party has been a more complete failure, so far as carrying out its promises is concerned, and yet my hon. friend remains absolutely unshaken, with a faith that laughs at impossibilities and cries it must be done.
A year ago last summer I was startled to find in my morning paper a report of a statement which had been made by my hon. friend in some small town in Alberta. He suggested that hundreds of millions of years ago providence had contemplated the idea of bringing into existence the province of Alberta and that there would be a great leader raised up to direct the destinies of that province. That leader was Mr. Aberhart. Hundreds of millions of years ago means at least two hundred million years. I do not know the condition of the earth at that distant date. It may have been without form and void; it may be that it was still in a stage of fervent heat. Perhaps it had begun to calm down a little and it may be the first crude forms of life had begun to develop. There may have been a slight movement, a bubble in the primordial ooze, and perhaps providence looking on, waved a hand and said:
There little creature, don't you cry;
You'll be Aberhartan by and by.
Even though I speak thus kindly of my hon. friend, I want also to call the attention to something else. He said today that we should work together with the greatest earnestness and fairness. He believed that we were all fan-minded men. I hope he will be able to live up to the creed which he has laid down. Last winter there was some discussion in this house about a bonus to be paid upon the production of sugar beets. I opposed that because I do not believe in tariffs or bonuses. If an industry in my constituency demanded a bonus, I would let it go and take my chance on being defeated. But I have heard on other occasions from friends of mine, who had it direct from the lips of the hon. member for Lethbridge, that he could not understand why I was opposed to the bonus being paid unless I was in the pay of the sugar interests. It is rather
The Address-Mr. Deachman

humorous to think that I would be in the pay of the sugar interests, but I suggest that my hon. friend ought to be careful.
I do not treat his statement with the sternness with which I might regard it if it came from a member of one of the older political parties, such as the Conservative or the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. After all a moral code is a product of slow growth. First, there are certain moral conceptions and it takes time to develop them. After all the Social Credit party is the youngest party in the House of Commons and it has not yet established its own code. It has not reached the condition where it can stand on honest convictions and antipicate that others will do the same. I suggest to my hon. friend that when he makes a statement such as that, he does not measure me; he measures himself. There is still some truth in the old couplet:
Now, as of old, Mail by himself is priced,
For thirty pieces Judas sold himself, not Christ.
I shall be glad now to turn to something more entertaining. The Conservative party is developing new leaders, and I am glad to see them. I would not for one moment suggest that I should be glad to see the old leader disappear, because after all the older he gets, the more I like him. Prior to 1935, when my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) laughed at all, he laughed at other people. In 1936, having thrown off the burden of office, he laughed spontaneously and naturally. In 1937 he laughed with others. From personal contact and from what I have heard from others, this year he laughs at himself. He must have had abundant reason to laugh at himself when he went home last night.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) has moved down closer to the front. I congratulate him. He is getting nearer to the throne, and I do not think he will ever get very far away from it. He ran away a little too far last summer, but the results were not happy. Then we have the outside leader of the Conservative party, a new man who has come upon the scene. I do not know whether he is the heir apparent, the heir presumptive or merely the pretender to the throne. He made a speech some time ago in Toronto upon which I must congratulate him. That speech contained some sentences which convinced me that I have converted him and that he now has some doubt as to the value of tariffs. A Conservative who has the dawning of doubt with regard to tariffs

is a valuable asset to the Dominion of Canada at the present time. We ought to welcome him to our midst. I am not sure that the conversion is complete, because his speech contains some strange dogmas. However, it is a very interesting speech and I should like to read a few sentences from it. He said:
In the beginning, the disadvantages of the national policy eclipsed its advantages. To build a Canada of great and equal opportunity meant hard work, especially at the outset;-
I agree with that. He continues:
-meant hardship, especially to the primary beneficiaries of freer trade. Our infant industries needed protection, if they were to prevail. Our labour needed protection, if it was to survive. But the foundations of a higher standard of living for the future, meant at that time, higher costs of living to the consumer. The producer of natural products paid twice over.

speechtext: Who said that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Herridge, the
former minister to the United States, the aspirant to the throne. Where is the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), the man who occasionally whispers an invocation for higher protection? Where is the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol)? Where is the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) ? Mr. Herridge speaks as a father who is chastizing his child and says: I hate to do this; it hurts me more than it does you, but it will be good for you in the end. His speech continues:
This was unavoidable, if you like. But none the less it was a strain upon the scanty resources of a pioneer community. It is to the eternal credit of Canadians that they saw the vision of a greater Canada, and endured.
I can imagine the members of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association enduring while they were permitted to charge the consumer two prices for the things that they had to sell. In order to build a Canada of great and equal opportunity, it was necessary to divide the country into two classes-even the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) was not accused yesterday of doing that-those who received payment and those who paid the bills. There is another touching passage here:
So up went the tariff, undoubtedly beyond that point where ends the public welfare and begins those high profits of special privilege which feast upon the public welfare.
And thus the tariff became a wall dividing east and west, industry and the primary producer, labour and the farmer. It ceased to be protection and became the perversion of the high morality of Canada first.
The Conservative party put up tariffs. It misemployed a noble principle.
Isn't that good?-the noble principle being that of charging the consumer two prices.
The national policy became discriminatory.

The Address-Mr. Deachman
It was born that way.
Admit it gracefully.
I wonder if my Conservative friends will admit gracefully that the national policy became discriminatory-no, not "became" but always was. Then he goes on to say:
Therefore, when labour is protected the farmer must be protected likewise.
It took them sixty years to find that out. It was twenty-four years before they realized the truth about reciprocity, and even then they could not vote for it. But it took them sixty years to realize that the farmer must-be protected alike with labour. It goes on:
And so his turn comes round at last. His protection is also a minimum wage. His minimum wage will be a minimum price level. In this way, labour and the farmer unite and become the joint guardians of our security.
I wonder if you could ever find a more delightful thing than that. The manufacturer, the protected interests, are still to be permitted -to exploit the community. No change in that. But the government is to undertake -the task of guaranteeing the prices of the products which the farmer produces, and so we will have industry exploiting the farmer and the government recompensing the farmer for the exploitation of industry. That is the new protection; that is the new national policy. Well, that will not last very long so far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned, but it does bring to the attention of the house a very serious matter. Even the Conservative party realizes the danger which confronts this country in connection with agriculture, and that is a story which I now desire to present.
For sixty years we have budgeted fairly steadily for depressed agricultural conditions. We have the fruits of that situation today. The average farmer in the province of Ontario -I am dealing now with the Ontario farmer because I happen to represent an Ontario constituency, but what I am going to urge in regard to the Ontario farmer ought to be applicable to the other provinces, although in the present circumstances Ontario is the pick of the bunch. Conditions here are better than in the other provinces, partly because of natural advantages, climatic conditions and so forth. The average farmer in the province of Ontario, according to the census of 1931, had an investment of $7,273. He had 119 acres of land. The value of his production per farm was $1,585 in 1930; that is gross production and takes no account of the cost of production or of the cost of living. It represents the value of the products produced on the farm, available for sale or for
consumption on the farm. In 1932 the value
of production had sunk to $964; that is, it declined by $621 in two years.
Permit me to say this for the benefit of my Conservative friends: This problem is too big to make it a partisan issue, and I am not charging the former government with the entire responsibility for the decline in the value of farm products which took place during these two years.
In 1936 the value of farm production had risen to $1,335, still a decline from 1930, but a substantial increase of $371 over the low level of 1932. I am going to be fair in this also, and say that the government cannot take the full credit for that increase, because part of it was the result of natural causes, and agriculture is still left in a depressed condition, which is something still to be faced.
As I have pointed out, that was the gross return. Then the farmer had to pay taxes on his farm, averaging $100. He had to buy feed, costing $80; fertilizer, $15; spraying materials, $3; seed, $24; power and light, $6; labour, including board for labour, $155. Then there should be an allowance for maintenance and operating expenses of implements, including gas, oil, twine, repairs, and so forth, which would amount to at least $100. Threshing would average $25, and the depreciation on his buildings and equipment would amount to at least $165. With an investment in his farm of $7,200, he ought to be entitled to five per cent interest, and if you add all these items of expense together, you have $973 of expenses on that farm. If the farmer was not getting interest on the money invested, he was paying interest on a mortgage, and if all these items are deducted from his income of 1936 the average farmer's net income in the province of Ontario was $362, or less than one dollar per day.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what you are going to do for an industry which has sunk so low that the total earnings, per farmer, are $360 a year. That is less than the pay which this government gives an office boy starting to work in the government service. Is there courage enough in parliament to say and to do something about this? Do you not think we have a problem there, a tremendous problem, as it exists at the present time? I wonder what we are going to do about it.
Let me put it another way. Let us take it upon an index basis. It is difficult to compare farm earnings with industrial wages, and in this case remember that I go only so far as an index will go. You must consider it as an index and nothing else, but yet it is an indication of real conditions.

The Address-Mr. Dcachman

Taking industrial wages at 100, and farm earnings at 100, in 1926, we can come to a fair approximation of farm earnings in the following years by comparing the relative prices which the farmer received for his products with the wages which the industrial worker received. There is no substantial variation in the volume of farm production during those years, and the reward of the farmer is dependent largely upon prices.
It stands this way: Industrial wages, 100 in 1926; 104-3 in 1932; 109-8 in 1935. Farm earnings, 100 in 1926; 83 in 1930; 59-5 in 1932. In other words, the earnings of the average farmer in Ontario in 1932 represented a decrease of 40-5 per cent from the level of 1926, while the earnings of labour went up during the same period by four per cent. Please note that I am not finding fault with the wages of labour. I am not saying that the earnings of labour are too high. I realize that while this was going on, while the farmer was paralysed, while his earnings had decreased over 40 per cent, labour was largely unemployed. But I raise this question-how far can labour go in increasing its wages while the farmer stands as he does. There is the difficulty which labour must face. You cannot have the rate of wages of labour steadily increasing over the years when you have at the same time the income of the farmer almost cut in two.
If we take again the cost of living and the value of farm produce at 100 in 1926, the cost of living in 1932 stood at 81-4 and the price of farm produce at 48-4.
These are conditions that call for the attention of the House of Commons, not of one political party only, but of all. I have given the prices of farm produce, and I want to point out that in the normal operation of the law of supply and demand the price of farm produce ought always to stand at a higher level than the price of manufactured products. There are certain basic reasons for this: First, mass production lowers the cost of manufacturing. Mass production is always possible in industrial production, but rarely possible in agriculture. Second, the mechanization of industry goes forward more rapidly than the mechanization of agriculture. Greater resources in capital and greater capacity for employment of technical experts in the development of research assist progress in manufacturing. Manufacturing is driven forward towards the lowering of costs of production-not necessarily of selling price-much more than agriculture. Third, fluctuations in volume of production and price are, to a large extent, under control in manufacturing. This gives greater stability and

permits lower costs. Fourth, production, per unit of capital invested, is greater in manufacturing than in farming. Fifth, interest rates are lower for the industrial borrower than for the agricultural producer. That ought to aid the manufacturer still further in producing at a low cost, while the farmer is naturally faced with a higher cost of production.
In view of all these facts we cannot expect that the price of farm produce will decline, as will the price of manufactured commodities; and for that reason the situation should be changing steadily in the direction of the farmer and not in the direction of the manufacturer. Why does this not happen? I am not going to be positive in that regard, because I want the house to explore and find out why, but I think there are some reasons which are quite obvious and the house ought to be able to discover them.
What is the result of the changes I have pointed out? Let me mention one fact which I regard as of great importance so far as farm life in Ontario is concerned. In 1931, according to the census, there were in rural Ontario, in the age group from twenty to twenty-nine, 115,000 males and 87,000 females. According to normal expectancy, taking the age group from twenty to twenty-nine-that is, the group in which most marriages take place-we should have had 124,709 males and 111,822 females in 1931. That was the normal expectancy. Actually there was a decrease of 9,000 males. The decrease in the number of females was 24,000. The young women had deserted the farms.
What is the reason for this? The reason is that the young woman was no longer a valuable economic unit on the farms of Ontario. The cost of living was high and she had to make a living. The female population moved away from the country to the city. Those of my hon. friends who are bachelors know, as perhaps the married men, too, know, that when the young women leave the country there inevitably follows a decline in the social activities of the people, for the young women are the life of the community, and so you have a serious social condition in the rural life of Ontario. Economic conditions have destroyed the normal balance of population. Moreover, there is a constant tendency for the young men to leave the country and go to the city. This is one of a number of aspects of the general situation that has developed as a result of agricultural conditions in Ontario. Another is the fact that our standards of education are declining, at any rate, so far as rural education is concerned.

Does the hon. gentleman say that education is declining.

The Address-Mr. Deachman

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I say that the standards of education in the rural communities are declining as compared with .the standards in the city schools.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will my hon. friend amplify that statement?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, gladly. My hon. friend, I understand, is a teacher, and I think he will realize that where salaries are low one is not likely to get the same standards of training among teachers as where higher salaries are paid; yet I find that among male teachers, in 1935-1936, the average salary in the country schools was $848, while in the urban schools it was $1,922. Even my hon. friend would not work as hard for $848 as for $1,922.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Is my hon. friend differentiating between the grade of diploma held by the teacher receiving $800 and the grade of diploma held by the teacher receiving $1,900?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What I have given has reference to public schools, and if .there was a difference in the matter of diplomas it only shows, what I am contending, that the country school cannot afford the high-salaried teachers who are employed in the cities. There are, in Ontario, something like 750 schools in which the average attendance is less than ten, and I venture to suggest that my hon. friends will appreciate how extremely difficult it is to provide the same high standards of education in such schools as exists in city schools, which have the advantage of better equipment. Inevitably, where there is a decline in rural wages, the earnings of the farmers, the standard of education will decline, not because the people want it to decline but because there is not the economic capacity to pay teachers.
I come to the question of remedies. I shall not discuss this question, because all I want the house to do is to realize the problem. I should like hon. members to appreciate the problem from the economic standpoint and to give full consideration to this fact, that if the entire rural population of Canada, or of the province of Ontario, must expect a low level of recompense for its work, then it follows inevitably that the burden will be felt by industries which will lack purchasing power; it will be felt by the railways; it will be felt in every phase of our life in Canada.
It is exceedingly difficult to obtain the facts. The story I have given to-day is not very clear, it is not very definite, because the facts are not available upon which to base a conclusion. Do hon. members realize that the latest available record of earnings of
51052-6A
farmers goes back to 1920 when the index of prices was 160 as against SO to-day? There were some reports prepared in 1931-32 by the Ontario Agricultural College. I endeavoured to get these reports but have not yet been able to obtain them as their circulation was banned by the government of Ontario at that time because the story they told was too tragic. They did not want the facts to be known. The same thing has occurred in the United States; when they start to investigate the living standards of the farmer the investigation collapses before it gets very far. But I contend that we ought to have these results.
Many will dispute these contentions in regard to the condition of the farmer. Some say: After all, the farmer is not trying to make a living; he is trying to live a life; he has a house of his own and all that. But I ask the government to give some time and attention to the problem. Let us make an analysis of the earnings on one hundred sample farms in Ontario, and a number of farms in other provinces. Let us take a fair selection, get the record and examine the facts. This would be a simple matter; we could use the facilities provided by our district agricultural representatives. It is possible to adopt a simple form of accounting and find out what the farmer earns. With a record like that, continued over a number of years, I am positive that we would have sufficient facts to convince any party or any government that the big problem before the people of Canada to-day is not, as some people say, the railway problem; it is not the unemployment problem; it is none of these problems-the real problem is to bring the standards of agricultural life up to such a point that when this nation goes forward-under a Liberal government, I hope, if a Liberal government is faithful to its trust, but otherwise under some other government-it will go foiward by a united movement all along the line, not simply raising by artificial means the reward of the few. while others are compelled to pay the added cost. I read from the address of the Hon. W. D. Herridge given in Toronto recently. I cannot agree with it. I do not think the problem can be solved in the way Mr. Herridge suggests, by a fixed price for agricultural products. There is no hope that way. I believe the movement should be towards freedom. Emerson said:
The basis of political economy is non-interference. The only safe rule is found in the self-adjusting meter of demand and supply. Do not legislate. Meddle and you snap the sinews with your sumptuary laws-give no bounties.

The Address-Mr. Deachman
I pass that on to my friend the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore).
Make equal laws and secure life and property. Open the door of opportunity to talent and virtue and they will do themselves justice and property will not be in bad hands. In a free and just commonwealth property rushes from the idle and imbecile to the industrious, brave and persevering.
I would not subscribe to all that; yet it is a safer, surer guidance than sumptuary laws, planned economy, fascism, communism or any other ism. But with a measure of freedom, helped to some extent by the correcting influence which government can exert, I am sure that standards of living for the farmer can be raised and he can be brought to an equality with the rest of the people of the dominion. If we fail in accomplishing this we have not solved the one great problem facing Canada. It must be settled or life itself has failed in this great nation.
